notes.meaning: Ahithophel asks Absalom for twelve thousand soldiers so he can chase David that very night. He knows speed is the key to winning, because David has not yet had time to rest or gather an army. By offering to lead the chase himself, he shows total confidence in his plan.

Ahithophel plans to attack David when he is exhausted and completely unprepared. A sudden strike in the dark would cause panic and make David's followers run for their lives. His goal is to kill only the king, ending the conflict without a large civil war.

Ahithophel promises to bring all the people over to Absalom once David is dead. He uses flattering language to treat Absalom as the true leader already. By taking only David's life, he claims the whole nation will quickly settle into peace.

Absalom and the leaders of Israel agree that Ahithophel's plan sounds wise and practical. The leaders are eager for a quick victory, even though it means murdering the king who had led them for decades. Blind ambition leads them to accept a cold-blooded scheme.

Absalom surprisingly asks to hear what Hushai has to say before making a final choice. God quietly guides Absalom's thinking here, leading him to doubt a plan that everyone else already approved. It shows that God can confuse the minds of powerful rulers to protect his servants.

Absalom explains Ahithophel's advice to Hushai and asks if they should follow it. He invites Hushai to give his honest opinion. Hushai is David's secret ally, and this question gives him the exact opening he needs to help save the king.

Hushai boldly states that Ahithophel's advice is not good this time. He avoids insulting Ahithophel's general wisdom, which makes his critique sound thoughtful and fair. This clever answer catches Absalom's attention right away.

Hushai reminds Absalom that David and his troops are seasoned fighters who will be as fierce as a mother bear robbed of her cubs. David is also an experienced commander who would never sleep out in the open with regular soldiers. Hushai plays on Absalom's fear of his father's battle skills.

Hushai argues that David is likely hiding in a cave or ravine, waiting to launch a surprise counter-attack. If Absalom's advance force loses even a few men early on, rumors will spread that the new king's army has been crushed. Hushai knows that bad news travels fast and breaks morale.

Hushai warns that even the bravest soldiers will lose all courage if they face an early setback. The whole nation respects the reputation of David and his veteran warriors. Hushai paints a scary picture to make Absalom hesitate and delay the chase.

Hushai suggests gathering an enormous army from the entire nation, from north to south, before going to war. He also flatters Absalom by urging him to lead this massive army in person. This idea sounds grand, but its real purpose is to buy David precious time to escape and regroup.

Hushai promises that a huge army will drop on David like heavy morning dew covers the grass. With such overwhelming numbers, not a single one of David's men will survive. This vivid picture appeals to Absalom's pride and desire for total glory.

Hushai exaggerates even more, claiming that if David hides inside a walled town, the army will pull the entire city into the valley with ropes. His boastful language is meant to dazzle Absalom's vanity. It makes Absalom picture an easy, dramatic triumph.

Absalom and his leaders decide that Hushai's counsel is better than Ahithophel's. The writer explains that the Lord Himself caused this choice so Absalom's rebellion would be ruined. God proves that human cleverness cannot succeed against His sovereign will.
Hushai immediately meets with Zadok and Abiathar the priests to share what happened in the council. He tells them both Ahithophel's plan and his own. He wastes no time getting the spy network moving.

Hushai tells the priests to warn David not to camp near the desert river crossings that night. Even though Absalom liked Hushai's plan, minds could change at any moment. David needs to cross the Jordan River right away to stay safe from a surprise attack.

The priests' sons, Jonathan and Ahimaaz, wait at the spring of En-rogel just outside the city walls. A servant girl goes back and forth to bring them the news without raising suspicion. They stay outside Jerusalem because entering would invite Absalom's guards to arrest them.
A young boy spots the two messengers and reports them to Absalom. The young men run quickly toward Bahurim to escape capture. There, an ally lets them climb down into a dry well inside his courtyard.

The man's wife lays a cloth over the opening of the well and spreads crushed grain on top. To any passerby, it looks like she is simply drying her grain in the warm sun. Her quick thinking completely hides the two messengers underneath.

Absalom's soldiers arrive at the house and ask where the two runners are. The woman sends the soldiers on a wild goose chase by telling them the men had already crossed the stream. After searching nearby and finding nothing, the pursuers give up and return to Jerusalem.

Once the search party leaves, Jonathan and Ahimaaz climb out of the well and sprint to King David. They deliver Hushai's urgent warning and describe Ahithophel's deadly advice. They urge David to cross the river immediately without any delay.

David listens to the warning and leads his people across the Jordan River during the night. By sunrise, every single person with him has crossed safely to the other side. Not one person was left behind or lost in the darkness.

Ahithophel realizes that his rejected advice will lead to Absalom's defeat and his own execution as a traitor. He rides home, puts his family affairs in order, and takes his own life. The smartest counselor in the nation meets a tragic end because he used his wisdom for evil.

David makes his way to the fortified town of Mahanaim on the east side of the Jordan. Meanwhile, Absalom spends time assembling his huge army and eventually crosses the river in pursuit. The delay gives David the exact breathing room he needs.

Absalom replaces Joab by naming Amasa as commander of his army. The family record shows that Amasa and Joab are first cousins, and both are nephews of David. The upcoming battle is not just a national war, but a painful conflict between close relatives.

Absalom and his army march into the region of Gilead and set up camp. This area lies east of the Jordan River and puts them close to David's stronghold. The stage is now set for a major showdown between father and son.

When David reaches Mahanaim, three prominent local leaders come out to greet him. Shobi the Ammonite, Machir from Lo-debar, and Barzillai from Gilead offer their loyalty to the king. In his darkest hour, God provides David with loyal friends in an unexpected place.

These three leaders supply David's followers with beds, bowls, pots, and plenty of nourishing food like wheat, roasted grain, honey, cheese, and meat. They know the travelers are hungry, thirsty, and worn out from their fast march through the wilderness. God uses the kindness of these neighbors to care for His exhausted people.
